Wheat straws‑derived hierarchical porous carbon as electrode 
material for supercapacitor
Zhenjuan Zang1 · Xiaolong Zhang2 · Baoshan Xia1 · Kelong Cao1 · Jinfeng Li1 · Qingguo Chen1
Received: 4 January 2025 / Accepted: 1 April 2025
© The Author(s) 2025  OPEN
Abstract
Hierarchical porous carbon materials hold great potential in electrochemical energy storage, yet their efficient fabrica-
tion still faces numerous challenges. Herein, we successfully prepared hierarchical porous carbon materials with high 
specific surface area, broad pore size distribution, and interconnected pore structures by direct co-pyrolysis of wheat 
straw and potassium hydroxide, leveraging the natural reticular structure of wheat straw. As an electrode material for 
symmetric supercapacitors, CS-800 exhibited excellent electrochemical performance, retaining 96.94% of its initial capac-
ity after 20,000 cycles at the current density of 1 A g⁻1 and achieving nearly 100% Coulombic efficiency. Furthermore, to 
expand its application scope, we assembled a zinc-ion capacitor using CS-800 as the cathode, which delivered a specific 
capacity of 173 mAh g⁻ 1 at a current density of 1 A g⁻ 1. The hierarchical porous structure and interconnected channels 
significantly enhanced ion transport and storage capabilities and optimized the adsorption and desorption processes 
of charge carriers. This study demonstrates that the preparation of high-value-added electrode materials from biomass 
waste holds broad application prospects.
Keywords Wheat straw · Hierarchical porous network carbon materials · Energy storage · Supercapacitors
1 Introduction
With the development of economy and the progress of science and technology, the energy demand is increasing day 
by day, which forms a serious contradiction with the increasingly depleted fossil resources [1]. At the same time, using a 
large amount of fossil energy has caused serious pollution to the environment. With the improvement of environmental 
awareness, human beings have higher requirements for energy use [2 ]. Therefore, we should focus on how to improve 
energy efficiency and develop clean and renewable new energy, such as pure electric vehicles. In this context, new energy 
storage and conversion devices with high energy efficiency, high energy and power density, and green environmental 
protection have received great attention and development [3]. Among them, supercapacitors have great market potential 
in hybrid vehicles, electronic equipment, military technology, and other fields due to their advantages of higher power 
density, high charge and discharge efficiency, large specific capacitance, and good cycle durability [4 ].
Supercapacitors are high-performance energy storage devices that work through the electric double-layer effect 
or redox reactions. Electric Double-Layer Capacitors (EDLCs) store energy by adsorbing ions on the electrode surface 
to form a double layer, while pseudocapacitors rely on fast redox reactions or Faradaic charge transfer in the electrode

materials [5]. Carbon materials play a crucial role in supercapacitors [6]. Moreover, the porous structure of carbon materi-
als facilitates ion transport, further improving the performance of the supercapacitors [7 ]. Their good chemical stability 
and corrosion resistance also extend the lifespan of the supercapacitors [8]. Therefore, with these characteristics, carbon 
materials have become the ideal choice for supercapacitor electrodes and have propelled the widespread application of 
supercapacitors in the field of energy storage. Biomass is the most abundant renewable carbon source in nature, with a 
rich variety of physical and chemical structures [8]. The rational development and utilization of natural biomass and waste 
biomass resources to produce porous carbon materials can not only achieve high-value utilization of biomass, but also 
effectively alleviate resource shortages and environmental pollution caused by the use of fossil resources [9]. Therefore, 
based on the concept of sustainable development, using abundant and renewable biomass as precursors to synthesize 
eco-friendly carbon materials and applying them in the energy storage field will have broad application prospects [2 ].
In this study, we successfully prepared hierarchical porous carbon materials via direct co-pyrolysis of natural wheat 
straw with potassium hydroxide. The electrochemical properties of these materials as electrodes for symmetric super -
capacitors and zinc-ion capacitors were systematically investigated. The symmetric supercapacitor based on CS-800 
exhibited a high specific capacitance of 145 F g⁻1 at a current density of 1 A g⁻1. Moreover, after 20,000 cycles, the device 
showed almost no significant performance degradation, demonstrating remarkable cycling stability. When the mass 
loading is 7.1 mg cm⁻ 2, the electrode exhibits a low voltage drop and high capacity retention, demonstrating promis-
ing potential for practical applications. To further expand its application scope, we assembled zinc-ion hybrid capacitor 
(ZIHCS) using CS-800 as the cathode, which achieved a specific capacity of 173 mAh g⁻ 1 at a current density of 1 A g⁻ 1. 
The results indicate that the coexistence of micropores and mesopores in the porous microstructure significantly impacts 
the rate performance and cycling stability of supercapacitors. These findings provide new insights and directions for 
further enhancing the performance of future supercapacitors.
2  Experimental section
Material and Chemicals: The fresh wheat straw used in the experiment was purchased from Shandong Province, China. 
Analytically pure Potassium hydroxide (Macklin, Analytically pure), hydrochloric acid (Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., 
Ltd., analytically pure). All solutions were prepared with ultra-pure water (18.2 MΩ  cm−1  purity, Millipore water purifica-
tion system).
Preparation of hierarchical porous carbon materials: 4 g wheat straw was ground and mixed with 2 g KOH. The 
mixture was pre-carbonized at 300 °C for 1 h at the heating rate of 3 ℃  min−1  in nitrogen atmosphere and then heated to 
the final carbonization temperature (600–800 °C) at a heating rate of 5 °C  min−1  for 1 h. The resulting black solid powder 
was washed with distilled water to the PH value of about 6–7. Finally, the samples were dried in a vacuum oven at 105 ℃ 
for 12 h. The final obtained sample was named CS-X, and X represented the final carbonization temperature. The sample 
pyrolyzed at 800 °C without KOH activation was used as a reference and designated as WS.
Structural characterization: The morphology and structure of the samples at room temperature (25 °C) were char -
acterized by Field emission frozen transmission electron microscope (FEI Tecnai F20) and scanning electron microscopy 
(SEM 5000) matched with high-throughput biological sample vacuum transfer device (Anhui ZEPTOOLS Technology Co., 
Ltd.). The crystal structure of the materials was carried out on an X-ray powder diffractometer (XRD, PANalytical X-Pert 
PRO MPD). The degree of graphitization of carbon materials was analyzed by Raman spectroscopy (Raman, Labram HR 
Evolution). The specific surface area and pore size distribution data were measured by a physical adsorption analyzer 
(Micromeritics, TriStarII3020).
Electrochemical Measurements: The supercapacitor performance of the samples was evaluated at room temperature 
using an electrochemical workstation. The electrodes were prepared by uniformly mixing 80 wt.% active material, 10 
wt.% acetylene black, and 10 wt.% polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) binder. The mixture was then coated onto nickel foil 
with a diameter of 10 mm and vacuum-dried for 12 h at 80 °C. Whatman glass fiber membrane was used as the separa-
tor, and the electrolyte consisted of 6 M KOH/2 M ZnSO₄. The supercapacitors were assembled using a CR2025 button 
cell casing. The electrochemical performance of the devices was assessed at room temperature using electrochemical 
workstation (Metrohm, AUTOLAB) and multi-channel battery tester (Neware Battery Test System).

3  Results and discussion
3.1  Morphology and microstructure of CS
The wheat straw-derived hierarchical porous carbon materials were characterized using Scanning Electron Microscopy 
(SEM) and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) (Figs.  1 and 2). Distinct microstructural differences were observed 
among the four samples. CS-700 and CS-800 displayed richer pore structures and interconnected network pores, which 
are beneficial for ion transport and storage. In contrast, CS-600 exhibited an underdeveloped porous structure, likely 
due to the lower activation temperature that failed to produce abundant pore defects. WS, which lacked the effect of 
the activator, showed minimal porous structure. The TEM images of CS-700 and CS-800 (Fig.  2c, d) revealed abundant 
defect features, which can provide active sites and enhance surface pseudocapacitance.
The porosity characteristics of the prepared carbon materials were further investigated through nitrogen adsorp -
tion–desorption measurements at 77 K. As shown in Fig. 3a, the adsorption isotherms of CS-700 and CS-800 exhibit Type 
IV behavior with a hysteresis loop [11]. In contrast, WS and CS-600 show Type I adsorption behavior without a hysteresis 
loop [4], indicating the absence of mesopores and macropores. Among these, CS-700 has the largest specific surface area 
(2210  m2 g⁻1), which may be attributed to the formation of more micropores after KOH activation. As the carbonization 
temperature increased to 800 °C, the increase in pore size led to a slight decrease in specific surface area. However, the 
pore size distribution curve (Fig. 3b) shows that CS-800 exhibits a hierarchical porous structure with different pore sizes. 
The presence of numerous mesopores significantly facilitates the adsorption and desorption of K⁺ (Stokes radius of K⁺ is 
3.6 Å) [12] and [Zn(H₂O) ₆] 2⁺ (with a diameter of 8.6 Å) [13], providing a large active surface area for charge storage. This 
enhances the utilization of storage space, accelerates charge transfer rates, and thus significantly improves the charge 
storage capacity [4].
The crystalline nature of the prepared carbon materials can be confirmed through the detection of characteris-
tic peaks in the XRD patterns. The XRD spectrum shows that CS-T exhibits a broad and weak diffraction peak near 
23°, corresponding to the (002) reflection of amorphous graphite carbon, while WS shows a relatively strong (002) 
peak (Fig.  4a) [14]. As the pyrolysis temperature increases, the intensity of the diffraction peak weakened and its 
width broadened, indicating that the carbon structures of CS-700 and CS-800 tend to become more amorphous.

In contrast, the graphite structures of WS and CS-600 exist in the form of short-range ordered graphite crystallites 
[14], which is closely related to their fewer defects and underdeveloped porous structures. The combination of 
abundant porosity and amorphous carbon provides a larger active surface area for ion storage, thereby facilitating 
more efficient ion storage [15].
The degree of graphitization and structural evolution of the hierarchical porous carbon materials were analyzed 
by Raman spectroscopy. The peak fitting results of the Raman spectra are shown in Fig.  4b, and the calculation 
results are presented in Fig.  4c. The  D1 band at approximately 1310 cm⁻ 1 reflects the presence of  sp3-hybridized car -
bon and the extent of defects in the material [16]. The G band at around 1580 cm⁻ 1, associated with  sp2-hybridized 
carbon, is commonly used as an indicator for quantitatively assessing defect density and the degree of lattice dis-
order [13]. The  D3 band at approximately 1490 cm⁻ 1 represents amorphous carbon structures [13]. Additionally, the 
 D4 peak near 1200 cm⁻ 1 is related to the vibrational modes of C = C bonds in the carbon material [17]. A higher  ID/IG 
ratio indicates a higher degree of disorder in the porous carbon, while a lower  ID/IG ratio suggests a higher degree 
of graphitization [18]. Specifically,  ID1/IG and  ID4/IG represent the defect degrees of graphite edges and polyene 
structures, respectively, and ID3/IG indicates the content of amorphous carbon in the material [19]. Overall, as the 
pyrolysis temperature increased from 600 °C to 800 °C, the  ID3/IG value gradually decreased, while the  ID1/IG value 
showed an increasing trend. This indicates that amorphous carbon was transformed into carbonaceous structures 
with more edge defects, which is beneficial for the intercalation and deintercalation of charge ions.

3.2  Electrochemical characteristics
The electrochemical properties of the prepared samples were analyzed using cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electro -
chemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) in a three-electrode system within 6 M KOH electrolyte (Fig.  5a, b). Among 
them, CS-800 exhibited the highest specific capacitance and the lowest charge transfer resistance, which can be 
mainly attributed to the large accessible surface area achieved through good micropore volume and interconnected 
conductive mesopore pathways.
Additionally, the electrochemical characteristics of CS-800 were further investigated by fabricating button-type 
symmetric supercapacitor with CS as the electrode in 6 M KOH electrolyte. As shown in Fig.  5c, the CV curves of the 
CS-800-based supercapacitor displayed rectangular features characteristic of EDLC behavior over the scan rate range 
of 2–200 mV s⁻ 1. Even at higher scan rates (100 and 200 mV s⁻ 1), the CV curves maintained nearly rectangular shapes, 
indicating rapid charge propagation and efficient ion transport within the electrodes. This excellent performance at 
high scan rates confirms the high-power capability of the porous carbon material. Figure  5d shows the galvanostatic 
charge–discharge (GCD) curves of the button-type symmetric supercapacitor at different current densities ranging 
from 0.5 to 20 A g⁻ 1. The electrode exhibits symmetrical charge–discharge curves, demonstrating a low IR drop at 
high current densities and excellent electrochemical reversibility. The calculated specific capacitances are 148, 145, 
138, 135, 133, and 123 F g⁻ 1 at current densities of 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, and 20 A g⁻ 1, respectively. As the current density 
increases, the specific capacitance gradually decreases, primarily due to insufficient diffusion of electrolyte ions on 
the electrode surface caused by rapid charging, which limits the full utilization of the electrode material.
As shown in Fig.  5f, the specific capacitance of the symmetric supercapacitor based on CS-800 in this study was 
compared with various porous carbon materials reported in recent literature[10, 20– 24], demonstrating a significant 
improvement in performance. Additionally, to verify its excellent rate performance, the symmetric supercapacitor 
based on CS-800 was tested for 20 cycles at current densities of 1, 2, 5, 10, and 20 A g⁻ 1 (Fig.  5e). When the current 
density was restored to 1 A g⁻ 1, there was no significant decrease in specific capacitance compared to the initial 
value. Importantly, the carbon electrode maintained high Coulombic efficiency at different current densities. Thus, 
the symmetric supercapacitor based on CS-800 not only exhibits excellent specific capacitance but also superior 
rate performance. EIS analysis revealed that the symmetric supercapacitor based on CS-800 has low charge transfer 
resistance (Rct) and diffusion resistance (Rs) (Fig.  5g), indicating rapid charge transfer capability and efficient ion dif -
fusion pathways. Moreover, the supercapacitor retained 96.94% of its initial capacity after 20,000 cycles at the current 
density of 1 A g⁻ 1 and achieved nearly 100% Coulombic efficiency (Fig.  5h), demonstrating excellent electrochemical 
stability. The Ragone plot (Fig.  5i) shows that the symmetric supercapacitor assembled with CS-800 achieves excel-
lent energy density of 21.2 Wh kg⁻ 1 at a power density of 800 W kg⁻ 1, which is superior to recently published data in 
terms of energy storage performance[10, 14, 20, 23, 25].
To further explore the practical application potential of the material, the electrochemical performance of the 
symmetric supercapacitor was analyzed at high mass loadings. No significant voltage drop was observed when the 
mass loading was below 7.1 mg cm⁻ 2 (Fig.  5j). The capacity retention rate was 56% for mass loadings ranging from

shows great application potential (Fig.  5k).
To further expand the application of CS-800 in the field of energy storage, we assembled ZHICs using CS-800 as the 
cathode, zinc foil as the anode, 2 M ZnSO₄ as the electrolyte, and Whatman glass fiber membrane as the separator. 
The electrochemical performance of the capacitor was investigated. Under a scan rate ranging from 5 to 200 mV s⁻ 1 
(Fig. 6a), the cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves exhibit quasi-rectangular features, indicating rapid electrochemical kinet -
ics. Meanwhile, the distinct redox peaks suggest the presence of pseudocapacitance, which significantly enhances the 
charge storage capacity. Figure 6c shows the galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) curves of the CS-800-based zinc-ion 
capacitor, which achieves a specific capacity of 173 mAh g⁻ 1 at a current density of 1 A g⁻1, significantly outperforming 
the results reported in recent literature (Fig.  6d) [26– 30]. Further kinetic analysis (Fig.  6b) indicates that when b = 0.5, 
the electrochemical process is diffusion-controlled, while when b = 1.0, it is capacitance-controlled. The fitted values of 
b = 0.92/0.89 suggest that the capacitor is primarily governed by rapid capacitive kinetics, with fast ion diffusion and 
transport capabilities. Additionally, further kinetic analysis (Fig. 6e–k) shows that at a scan rate of 5 mV s⁻1, the capacitive 
contribution accounts for 44% of the total capacity. However, when the scan rate increases to 200 mV s⁻1, the capacitive 
contribution sharply rises to 83%. This result reveals the rapid diffusion kinetics of  Zn2⁺ in CS-800, indicating that it can 
maintain efficient charge storage even at high rates.
4  Conclusions
In summary, hierarchical porous carbon materials were prepared via carbonization and activation of Wheat Straws. 
The impressive capacitive response of the optimal sample is strongly related to its unique features of composition and 
structure. The high surface area and hierarchically interconnected porous framework enable fast ion transport and thus 
achieve higher specific gravimetric capacitances of 145  Fg−1  at 1 A  g−1 , as well as excellent rate performance and cycle 
performance. When the mass loading is 7.1 mg cm⁻2, the electrode exhibits a low voltage drop and high capacity reten-
tion, demonstrating promising potential for practical applications. To further expand its application scope, we assembled 
zinc-ion hybrid capacitor (ZIHCS) using CS-800 as the cathode, which achieved a specific capacity of 173 mAh g⁻ 1 at a 
current density of 1 A g⁻ 1. The results indicate that the coexistence of micropores and mesopores in the porous micro -
structure significantly impacts the rate performance and cycling stability of supercapacitors. It indicates that it has great 
potential in practical applications. Therefore, it is a promising strategy for employing low-cost, eco-friendly biomaterials 
to synthesize advanced electrode materials for high-performance supercapacitors.
